# Narrator Framing — Cold Opens and Outros

## The frame

> status: ratified (D-0035, D-0036, D-0038)

Audio series first; fully voiced cast with foley; a (probably) omniscient narrator who
owns the cold open and the outro, with only bits in between as needed. The narrator
speaks from centuries out, through song, poetry, tapestry-readings, and history
quotes, sustaining a very oblique sense of a better future without ever showing the
narrator's own present. The whole is framed as a record decoded at a great remove
from the events — the Handmaid's Tale / found-manuscript trick.

## Cold opens

> status: ratified (D-0037, D-0045, D-0220)

Each cold open is a tone promise: a Taoist/zen-koan-like microcosm of the episode —
sometimes nearly impenetrable on first hearing — or the episode's arc in miniature as
fable, fairy tale, or legend; sometimes plain history or apocrypha. Not always
literal poetry. Always with the clear historical remove of quotation: the narrator is
reading something, dated and sourced in-world, in the manner of Dune's chapter
epigraphs. The koan's meaning should click into place only as the episode plays out.
Specimens live in [[in-world-texts]].

The spoken quotation defaults to two or three sentences, followed by a separate
named-source attribution. That is enough room for an image, complication, and turn;
one-line compression too easily collapses into a familiar real-world aphorism. The
epigraph still stays brief and oblique rather than becoming a miniature lecture.

## Outros

> status: ratified (D-0036)

The narrator returns to close: a brief reflection, a fragment of verse or record, a
quiet tightening of the episode's meaning into the long view — melancholy, humane,
obliquely hopeful. Music seals it (D-0039, [[audio-design]]).

## Mid-episode discipline

> status: ratified (D-0036, D-0179)

Between open and outro, the narrator intrudes only when audio genuinely needs it
(passage of time, the unshowable). The present action belongs to the cast and the
foley.

D-0179 clarifies the medium rule: "only when audio genuinely needs it" is not a
rare exception in the style of old-school radio-play sound painting. This piece is
closer to an audiobook with cast and foley. SFX is best-effort support, not a huge
semantic character, and it must not carry causal comprehension by itself. When a
listener would otherwise need to infer object relationships, off-mic state,
passage of time, or action gaps from ambiguous sound cues, the windowpane narrator
does that work plainly.

## No voice-description narration

> status: ratified (D-0218)

The author rule is absolute: “the narrator can never describe what people’s voices
sound like or how they said things.” Narrator copy therefore never supplies vocal
qualities, accents or phonetics, delivery adverbs, vocal metaphors, or indirect
how-said description. The ban includes prose that makes a person's words, sentences,
or speech “arrive,” “land,” or carry a described sound in place of describing the
voice directly.

This is a narrator-register ban, not a ban on the story acknowledging sound or bodily
cost. Character dialogue may mention voices. The narrator may state neutrally that
someone spoke, describe breathing and the physical price of speech or magic, and use
metaphors for the sounds of objects, animals, weather, or the natural world. Those
allowances may not be used to smuggle a description of human vocal delivery back into
the narration.

## Proposed refinements

> status: proposed

Unratified: recurring source-citation formulas ("From the third woven register of
the Drowned Parishes…") as an audio signature; the loom-clack and card-turn as the
narrator's signature foley.

## The narration registers

> status: ratified (D-0152, D-0176, D-0179)

The narrator speaks in layers, and the layers are ruled: his QUOTES — the koan
cold-opens and the outros — are one deliberate tone, his own. MOST NARRATION is
windowpane: clear glass, the story seen straight through it. And at rare moments
the register itself is allowed to reveal that he knows what is coming — the
scholar's tell, a sentence that could only be written by someone who has read the
whole chronicle. Those moments are spent, not scattered.

D-0176 tightens the windowpane: the narrator is largely invisible, third-person,
and largely omniscient by way of future artifacts and histories. The voice may quote
or gloss records from centuries downstream, but it may not turn toward the listener,
announce "the promise of the tale," or otherwise explain why the scene matters. A
good narrator frame feels like a scholar letting the record show, not a host
selling the episode.

D-0179 adds the complementary guardrail: largely invisible is not absent. The
narrator must carry orientation, causality, and continuity when the alternative is
asking SFX/foley to paint an overprecise picture. The house style rejects both
host-like overexplanation and radio-play overdependence on sound effects.

## No ticking clock

> status: rejected (D-0104)

The narrator's own era carries no live tension and no urgency device. "The world has
its story urgency. the narrator is more abstract." The lit-agent-era "why translate
these records now?" clock is dead; the narrator stays centuries-out, unhurried,
abstract.
